title: Nature's prescription
hook: as doctors prescribe cold baths, nature prescribes illness or loss; take it like medicine (Meditations 5.8)

segments.voice: Yesterday: what is wholly yours. Your line was what is mine. Which did you show: sincerity, dignity or endurance? Day five hundred sixty-six.

Physical therapy hurts. The stretch you're told to hold for thirty seconds feels like three minutes. The exercise for your knee is boring and sore. And yet you do it, more or less cheerfully, because someone you trust wrote it down and said: this will help. You don't argue with a prescription the way you argue with bad luck. Marcus Aurelius noticed that difference, and in the eighth entry of book five he tried to move the hard things in his life from one column to the other. Today: nature's prescription.
screen: `PHYSICAL THERAPY HURTS.` → `YOU DON'T ARGUE WITH A PRESCRIPTION.` → `NATURE'S PRESCRIPTION.`

segments.voice: First, the doctor. People say, Marcus writes, Asclepius prescribed this man horseback riding, or cold baths, or walking barefoot. Asclepius was the Greek god of healing, and sick people slept in his temples hoping for instructions in a dream. Marcus's world was full of such prescriptions. Second, nature's prescription. In the same way, he says, the nature of the whole prescribed for this person an illness, or a disability, or a loss. The word for prescribed is the same. The event is not random, in his view. It's fitted to you, the way a prescription is written for one patient. Third, two reasons to accept it. Marcus gives two. One: it happened to you, it was assigned to you, it's woven into your own life. Two: it serves the health of the whole universe, which he believed was one living order. You don't have to share his belief about the cosmos to feel the force of the first reason. This is your life, and this is in it. Fourth, take it like medicine. So, he says, accept what happens the way you accept what the doctor orders. Many prescriptions are bitter, and we welcome them anyway, hoping for health. Here's what this changes. You can't always choose whether hard things come. But you can choose which column they go in: bad luck, to be resented, or medicine, to be taken. Taken as medicine, a hard season becomes something you can work with. Marcus isn't saying it doesn't taste bitter. He's saying bitter isn't the same as wrong.
screen: `ASCLEPIUS PRESCRIBED A COLD BATH.` · `NATURE PRESCRIBED AN ILLNESS.` · `YOURS, AND PART OF THE WHOLE.` · `BITTER, BUT TAKEN FOR HEALTH.` · then, large: `THE PRESCRIPTION.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one hard thing in your life right now: an ache, a limit, a loss, a difficult person. Notice which column it's been in. Bad luck? Something to resent? Now, just for these breaths, try moving it to the other column. Picture it written on a prescription pad, with your name at the top. Ask: what might this be medicine for? Patience, humility, compassion? Take it, the way you'd take a bitter pill. The bell holds the time.
Nature's prescription. Marcus says as a doctor prescribes cold baths, nature prescribes illness or loss: take it as medicine, bitter but meant for health. Today's word.
Your line: the prescription. When something hard comes today, ask: what is this medicine for? Day five hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes reframe a hardship as in Meditations 5.8, asking what it might be medicine for, rather than treating it only as bad luck.

original.note: Greek, Asclepius, god of healing, whose prescriptions Marcus compares to what nature assigns.

trapdoor: what you thought: everything happens for a reason.
what it means: take hard things the way you take a doctor's orders: bitter, but accepted for health.
what a scholar hears: Asclepius's temples practiced 'incubation', sleeping there for healing dreams; Marcus's own physician Galen honored Asclepius.

notes: 5.8 paraphrased: as we say Asclepius prescribed horse exercise, cold baths, or going without shoes, so nature prescribed disease, mutilation, loss; two reasons to be content: it was done for you, prescribed and related to you, woven into your destiny; and it is a cause of the well-being and perfection of the whole; accept it as we accept what Asclepius prescribes, many things disagreeable but welcomed for the hope of health. Confirm. Marcus uses the same verb (suntasso) for both prescriptions: confirm.
Temple incubation at Asclepieia (e.g., Epidaurus, Pergamon): standard. Galen's devotion to Asclepius (he called himself the god's servant): confirm.
